approachQuestion.prompt: A live service receives n integer scores in arrival order. Return the k greatest scores in descending order, preserving duplicates. Its source supports one forward pass and cannot be rewound; after a score is delivered, the algorithm may retain its own values. Example 1: scores=[7,12,3,9,12,1,9,4], k=3 → [12,12,9]. Example 2: scores=[5,5,5,1,8,2], k=2 → [8,5]. Which approach returns the required list?
constraints: Each score is a signed 64-bit integer; comparisons take constant time.
Consume the source once in arrival order; it cannot be rewound. Do not alter the source. The algorithm may allocate and retain its own buffers.
Return exactly k scores in descending order; equal scores may appear in any order relative to one another.

options.text: Keep a min-oriented priority queue of at most k scores. Fill it with the first k values; for each later value, compare it with the smallest retained score and replace that score only when the new value is larger. Once the stream ends, arrange the retained k values in descending order.
options.feedback: The smallest retained value marks the current boundary: any later value no larger than it cannot enter the greatest k. The queue never needs to hold values that cannot affect the result.

options.text: Store every arriving score in an algorithm-owned array, sort that array in descending order after the single pass, and return its first k values.
options.feedback: This is valid because the algorithm-owned array is allowed and the source is consumed only once. It orders and retains every score although only k are returned; a bounded candidate set avoids that removable work and storage.

options.text: For each of the k output positions, scan the input for the greatest score not already selected, then mark that occurrence as used.
options.feedback: This method requires rewinding and rereading the source for each output position, but the stated stream permits only one forward pass. As written it cannot be carried out on this input; it is not merely a slower legal scan.

options.text: Insert all n scores into a max-oriented priority queue, then remove its maximum k times to form the answer.
options.feedback: This is correct, but it retains every score even though only k can be returned. Keeping only the current k candidates makes the stored state bounded by the requested result size.

feedback.reason: Focus on how many candidates must remain available after each new value arrives, and what the requested result requires you to retain.
details: Keep a min-oriented priority queue containing the current k greatest scores. Its root is the smallest score among those retained. Ignore a later score when it does not exceed that root; otherwise replace the root. Finally, order the retained scores from greatest to least.

The retained minimum is the weakest current top-k candidate. Replace it only with a larger arrival; duplicates still represent separate scores. Sorting all n arrivals stores and orders candidates that will never appear in the answer.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze the fixed method: read n scores once, keep a min-oriented priority queue with capacity k, insert until it contains k scores, and for each remaining score replace the root only when the score is larger. At the end, arrange the retained scores in descending order. Let n be the number of scores and k the requested result size.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. A queue insertion or root replacement may restore heap order; comparisons and score moves are constant-time. The final ordering is performed in place within the retained queue.
The returned k-element list is output and is excluded from auxiliary space. The input is excluded; count the priority queue and all other working storage.

options.text: O(n log(k+1)) time, O(k) auxiliary space
O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Heap repairs use log k height and the working queue retains k scores.
details: The first k values are inserted into the queue. Each of the remaining n−k values is compared with the root and may cause one root replacement; each queue adjustment involves at most the queue height. Ordering the retained k values takes no more than the stated overall bound. The queue contains at most k scores, and the final ordering is in place. The input and returned list are excluded. The bound is attained for k≥2 by scores [1,2,…,k,k+1,…,n]: every later score exceeds the current heap contents, replaces the root, and sifts to a leaf, taking Θ(log k); there are Θ(n) such replacements because k≤n/2. The final in-place ordering costs O(k log k), within the same bound, and the full queue occupies Θ(k) space. k=1 is outside this task's constraints; if included, the same method reduces to a linear scan with constant auxiliary space.

“O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This describes ordering a copy of all scores, while the fixed method maintains only k candidates. It overstates both the work and retained storage for the specified method.

“O(kn) time, O(k) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not rescan all n scores for each output position. Each incoming score is checked once, and only a possible queue replacement needs heap adjustment.

“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The time bound omits the cost of restoring heap order when a score enters or replaces a candidate. Its space bound also counts n values, although the queue is capped at k.

methodReveal.title: Maintain only the strongest k candidates
methodReveal.description: Keep a min-oriented priority queue containing the current k greatest scores. Its root is the smallest score among those retained. Ignore a later score when it does not exceed that root; otherwise replace the root. Finally, order the retained scores from greatest to least.
